Pulse
PULS
n. (the edible seeds of leguminous plants, as beans, lentiles, and peas; plain food, as opposed to rich fare)
Latin puls, a thick porridge or pottage, the staple grain-mash of the Roman poor. The word narrowed in English to the seeds themselves — beans, lentiles, peas — the plainest and least esteemed of ordinary food.

See also: Pulse

Biblical Definition

Daniel's test before the prince of the eunuchs is built entirely around this one humble word. Having purposed in his heart not to defile himself with the king's meat or wine, Daniel proposes an alternative so modest it barely counts as a request: Prove thy servants, I beseech thee, ten days; and let them give us pulse to eat, and water to drink. He does not ask for a theological exemption or a public confrontation; he asks for beans and water for ten days, and offers to let the results speak for themselves.

The result is the whole point of the chapter: at the end of ten days, the four young men fed on pulse alone appeared fairer and fatter in flesh than all the youths who ate the king's rich portion, and Melzar took away the king's meat and continued giving them pulse. Second Samuel uses the same word in an entirely different scene — parched pulse among the provisions brought to David's exhausted army in the wilderness, plain food doing plain, sustaining work for men in flight. Between the two scenes, pulse becomes an unlikely emblem of a single principle: that faithfulness in a small, unglamorous matter, kept without fanfare, can carry a strength that no rich table ever supplied.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): the edible seeds of leguminous plants, as pease, beans, and lentiles; food of a plain and simple kind.

expand to see more

PULSE, n. Leguminous plants, or their seeds, as beans, pease, and lentiles, used for food.

PORTION, n. A part or share allotted or distributed; especially, a share of food assigned to a person.

DEFILE, v.t. To make unclean or impure; to corrupt; to render ceremonially unfit.

PROVE, v.t. To try; to test by experiment or experience; to establish the truth of by trial.

FAIR, a. Beautiful; pleasing to the eye; also, of a healthy or well-favored appearance.

Key Scripture

Dan 1:8 — "But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the portion of the king's meat, nor with the wine which he drank: therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself."

Dan 1:12 — "Prove thy servants, I beseech thee, ten days; and let them give us pulse to eat, and water to drink."

Dan 1:16 — "Thus Melzar took away the portion of their meat, and the wine that they should drink; and gave them pulse."

2Sa 17:28 — "Brought beds, and basons, and earthen vessels, and wheat, and barley, and flour, and parched corn, and beans, and lentiles, and parched pulse,"

Modern Corruption

Plain, unglamorous obedience is treated as spiritually unimpressive next to visible sacrifice or public confrontation, when Daniel's whole test is built on beans and water quietly outperforming the king's own table.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain word; pulse still names the humblest grade of food. The principle worth recovering is how deliberately small Daniel's actual act of faithfulness was. He does not demand a public exemption from Babylon's whole court, does not stage a confrontation with Nebuchadnezzar, does not ask for anything except ten days and beans — and lets the outcome, not the gesture, do the persuading.

The chapter's verdict is unambiguous: the pulse-fed young men were fairer and fatter than the whole company fed on the king's portion, and their plain diet becomes the quiet, undeniable evidence behind everything Daniel accomplishes in the rest of the book. Faithfulness in the smallest and least impressive matter, kept without fanfare and proven rather than merely asserted, is exactly the pattern pulse is made to carry in this text.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew zeroa (H2235), seed, sown food; the general word behind the pulse Daniel requests, related to the Hebrew for sowing seed.

expand to see more

Hebrew zeroa (H2235) — that which is sown, seed, vegetable food; the word rendered “pulse” in Daniel 1:12, 16.

Hebrew ga'al (H1351) — to defile, to pollute; the verb behind Daniel's purpose not to defile himself with the king's meat.

Hebrew bachan (H974) — to try, to test, to prove; the verb behind Daniel's own request, Prove thy servants.

Hebrew bariy (H1277) — fat, well-fed, fleshy; the word describing the pulse-fed youths' appearance in Daniel 1:15.

Hebrew qaliy (H7039) — parched, roasted grain; the preparation named of the pulse brought to David's army in 2 Samuel 17:28.

Usage

"“let them give us pulse to eat, and water to drink” — Daniel's modest, testable request."

"“Melzar took away the portion of their meat... and gave them pulse” — the outcome that vindicated it."

"“parched corn, and beans, and lentiles, and parched pulse” — the same plain food sustaining David's army."
